stageLabel: The first song: collaboration and a modest return
shapeSentences: A young worker made his first song with a colleague after seeing a rival succeed, but publication brought very little money.
A first completed collaboration was real work even though its commercial result was small.
He remembered surprise at how little the song earned; the episode ends with a beginning, not a breakthrough.

facets.emotionalCore: Disappointment at a first creative project's small return, grounded in his remembered surprise at the earnings.
facets.decisionShape: Responding to another team's success by making a first song together, with one collaborator writing words and the other music.
facets.triggerEvent: A rival café's singing waiter and pianist had written a hit, prompting his own collaboration.
facets.agencyState: A singing waiter could contribute lyrics and work with the café pianist; publication was possible without a hit or a living wage.

biographicalFacts: Irving Berlin was born on May 11, 1888. His first published song, Marie from Sunny Italy, appeared in 1907, at eighteen or nineteen. In his attributed 1934 Radio Stars interview he recalled being a singing waiter and collaborating with the café pianist because a rival café's waiter and pianist had produced a hit. The original published score credits I. Berlin with words and M. Nicholson with music. The publisher was Jos. W. Stern & Co. Berlin recalled that their song was not a hit and that its small profit surprised him. The interview's thirty-odd cents describes a joint profit; it is not equated with an individual royalty. The episode is a first collaboration and modest publication, not a claim that earnings or confidence were secured.

beats.text: He was a singing waiter, about nineteen, when he worked on his first published song. The café's pianist worked with him.

beats.text: In his memory, competition between the cafés pushed him toward writing a song of his own. A rival song was already a hit.

beats.text: He and the pianist made a song together, with words by one and music by the other. He supplied the words.

beats.text: The result was a collaboration, not a song he had made entirely alone. His partner supplied the music.

beats.text: Their song was published, with both men's contributions credited on the sheet music. It was his first publication.

beats.text: The song did not become a hit, and he remembered being surprised by its small return. The profit was less than a dollar.

beats.text:
His name was Irving Berlin.

He wrote songs for singers, musical theatre, and films.

Your life is not theirs.

But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You are allowed to value a beginning that brought little reward.

You are allowed to need other people.
